transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Sofia Rivera (Redwood SE), Evan Cole (CTO, Monarch), Priya Narang (Lead ML Eng), Marcus Liu (SRE)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood behavior under combined long-context retention and high TPS streaming. Showed Console metrics, API fallthrough patterns, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Discussed VPC networking and timeouts, planned bench tests.

Topics: long-context fallthrough, streaming backpressure, per-connection inflight limits, timeouts, console traces, dedicated vs hosted fallback, KV cache eviction, Optimize tuning.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Jordan from Redwood, joining with Sofia. um, quick roll call?
[00:00:06] Evan: Evan here. Priya and Marcus are on.
[00:00:08] Priya: yep hi all.
[00:00:10] Marcus: Marcus here.
[00:00:12] Jordan: great. goal for today — demo our playbook when you have super long sessions (multiple 100ks of tokens) plus bursts of parallel traffic. show console traces, then run a short demo of streaming backpressure. Sofia will lead the technical bits.
[00:00:28] Sofia: hi, yeah i'll start with a quick topology diagram — we've got requests hitting the API gateway, routed to serving pools. important bits are: prefix (kay vee) cache, batching window, and per-connection inflight request caps. you'll see how those interact when a session keeps appending history.
[00:00:48] Evan: quick question — our current app holds about 120k tokens per user in cold storage but only streams last 40k to the model. we saw drop-offs when load spikes, is that the fallthrough you mean?
[00:00:58] Sofia: yes. fallthrough is the runtime dropping older context frames when the kv cache evicts — which can change the prompt context. we simulate two patterns: graceful fallthrough where we truncate and warn, and hard fallthrough where we reroute to a smaller variant.
[00:01:17] Priya: what's the threshold for eviction? is it bytes or token count?
[00:01:20] Sofia: mostly token-based, but also memory pressure on the GPU. the kernel selector will favor a quantized 8-bit path only if sequence length and GPU memory allow it. in practice we set soft and hard thresholds per model.
[00:01:36] Marcus: ok network stuff — if we do this in VPC, are we likely to hit socket limits causing half-closed streams? we had weird http/2 resets in our last run.
[00:01:44] Jordan: good flag. Redwood's default streaming uses chunked transfer over HTTP/1.1 and we also support server-sent events. on dedicated we can bump per-connection windows; but you still need to tune OS file-descriptor limits and load balancer timeouts.
[00:01:58] Sofia: i'll show an example trace.

[00:02:12] Sofia: (screen share) here's the console. left panel is per-model latency heatmap, center is active sessions. notice session ID 0x2b9f — it's a 220k token session with 18 concurrent inflight requests. look at the blue shaded area — that's continuous batching causing per-token latency to drop but increasing memory usage.
[00:02:34] Priya: are those inflight requests user-triggered or system retries?
[00:02:37] Sofia: user-triggered, parallel prompts from the same user for different sub-tasks. we allow multiple parallel streams per session up to a policy limit. beyond that we either queue or trigger a fallback to a cheaper variant.
[00:02:50] Evan: fallback — meaning we switch models automatically? can we pin a version?
[00:02:54] Jordan: yes you can pin. fallback is policy driven: for example, on memory pressure we route to 1) a quantized variant, 2) a shorter-context variant, or 3) a dedicated fallback lane on a different pool.
[00:03:05] Marcus: that sounds like race conditions waiting to happen — how do you keep output consistent?
[00:03:09] Sofia: great question. we surface a consistency score in the console and we link outputs to the model variant used. for strict consistency you can lock to a dedicated model and reserve sufficient GPU capacity.

[00:03:28] Jordan: ok demo time — we'll generate a stream that appends large system messages while also firing 500 concurrent tokens-per-second requests. you'll see backpressure and how the runtime sheds.
[00:03:40] Sofia: initiating script... (noisy typing)
[00:03:50] [00:03:50] Speaker 1: uh there's a small lag, buffering — oh yep, you can see the SSE connection flags.
[00:03:58] [00:04:00] Sofia: hitting 4.8k TPS across the pool, per-connection window at 32 inflight. you can see we start queuing at 00:04:12. the console shows a rising queue depth and a per-session latency tail.
[00:04:22] Priya: that tail spike is about how long?
[00:04:25] Sofia: peak tail went to ~2.1s per token for that session, average still ~120ms. our automatic fallback configured for this demo is a short-context variant which truncates to the last 32k tokens — that's the graceful option.
[00:04:39] Evan: what triggers the hard failover vs graceful?
[00:04:42] Sofia: hard is a threshold — e.g. if queue depth > X and memory > Y for Z seconds we do a deterministic hard failover to a compatible smaller architecture, otherwise we throttle and return 429s with an explicit Retry-After header.

[00:04:58] Marcus: will the client see partial responses mid-failover?
[00:05:01] Sofia: yes streams can be cut; we provide per-chunk metadata so clients can stitch or re-request. but you should design idempotent chunks or checkpointing.
[00:05:08] Priya: about timeouts — our infra enforces 60s idle LB timeouts. streaming sessions lasted longer in your demo, did you have keepalives?
[00:05:16] Jordan: we recommend explicit heartbeat frames every 25s and a TTL for session liveness in the control plane. also bump the LB timeout if you can. for VPC we collaborate on network policy to ensure long-lived sockets are kept alive.

[00:05:36] [00:05:36] Sofia: showing stack traces now — you can filter by error class. see this orange bar? that's backpressure shedding — number of requests dropped due to per-pool overload. click it and you get a playbook: steps to remediate and which metrics to watch.
[00:05:52] Evan: can that playbook be automated? like trigger an alert and auto-scale?
[00:05:56] Sofia: yes, you can connect autoscale rules or set a policy to automatically ramp burst capacity or spin up a dedicated lane. note that cold start of new nodes can affect latency, so we recommend warm standby for enterprise SLAs.

[00:06:12] Priya: what's the impact of prefix caching on long sessions? if we have a 200k token history but only last 20k is hot, does caching help?
[00:06:21] Sofia: yes — prefix caching keeps KV segments of the working set in GPU memory. if your working set is much smaller than total history, costs drop dramatically. but when your working set grows (e.g., whole 200k becomes active) you hit eviction and fallthrough behaviors.
[00:06:36] Marcus: any tooling to pre-compute compressed embeddings or snapshots to reduce token count?
[00:06:40] Jordan: Optimize includes suggestions: vector snapshots of old conversation turns, sparse summarization, and model quantization tradeoffs. we can run our Optimize profiler against your sample workload and produce a recommended config.

[00:06:58] [00:07:00] Sofia: i want to show a failure mode — when multiple sessions try to rehydrate a large context the KV cache experiences thundering-herd. here we simulate 12 sessions reloading a 180k context. watch the kernel selector flip to fallback.
[00:07:15] [00:07:16] Sofia: there — hard fallback activated at 00:07:22, sessions get routed to quantized-compat pool. notice logs show slight output divergence — that's expected due to quantization.
[00:07:30] Priya: how big is the divergence generally? our app is sensitive to wording.
[00:07:34] Sofia: on our tests divergence is small for many tasks (few percent), bigger for exacting tasks. Optimize can run a regression suite against your prompts to quantify.

[00:07:50] Evan: in production we care about cost — if we pin dedicated nodes to avoid divergence that could be pricey. what's the typical tradeoff?
[00:07:58] Jordan: yep it's cost vs consistency. dedicated for critical paths, hosted with intelligent fallback for best cost. Optimize will show cost per 1k tokens across strategies so you can pick a SLO tradeoff.

[00:08:12] Marcus: can we control which sessions are prioritized? like premium customers get reserved inflight slots?
[00:08:18] Sofia: yes — routing policies can tag sessions and prioritize them at the router. you can reserve preemptive slots in dedicated pools.

[00:08:30] [00:08:30] Sofia: switching to API logs — here's a trace where client 1 had a streaming connection and client 2 pushed a huge prefix, causing a per-pool memory spike. the runtime started issuing 429s with Retry-After of 4s. the client retried and we got a slight tail latency bump.
[00:08:50] Priya: do you recommend client-side exponential backoff?
[00:08:52] Jordan: yes exponential with jitter, and circuit-breaker patterns for repeated 429s or 5xxs. also instrument retry idempotency keys.

[00:09:04] Evan: any gotchas with HTTP/2 multiplexing? we want to multiplex many streams over a single connection for efficiency.
[00:09:10] Sofia: it's fine but the server still enforces per-stream inflight limits. with HTTP/2 a single OS connection can carry many streams but kernel-level memory quotas still apply; mixing very long-lived streams with short spikes can complicate scheduling.

[00:09:28] [00:09:28] Sofia: quick pivot — showing Optimize recommendations page. it suggests batching window tweaks and a 12k sequence micro-batching for your workload. toggles here will simulate projected cost and latency percentiles.
[00:09:44] Priya: can we run offline simulation against our traces?
[00:09:47] Jordan: yes — upload a sample trace (we'll accept gzipped JSON) and Optimize will run monte-carlo sims and return a config. that's what Sofia will run after this call.

[00:10:02] [00:10:02] Sofia: running a simulated 10-minute 5k TPS spike now — starting... watch the console.
[00:10:20] [00:10:20] Sofia: we hit sustained 5.1k TPS, queue depth spiked then plateaued due to our configured burst capacity. latency p95 rose from 220ms to 780ms during the peak then recovered.
[00:10:34] Marcus: curious — what's the recommended burst capacity for us?
[00:10:37] Sofia: depends on your budget. for Monarch we'd recommend 2x typical peak for 15 minutes as burst buffer, plus a warm standby for mission-critical traffic.

[00:10:52] Evan: one more on logs — can we export the raw chunk traces? we want to correlate with app-side telemetry.
[00:10:57] Jordan: yep full trace export supported, with an event id per chunk. we can anonymize PII if needed.

[00:11:10] Priya: security — SOC2/ISO audits, KMS integration for keys, audit logs for fallbacks?
[00:11:16] Jordan: we have SOC2 type II, optional HSM/KMS integration for Private deployments, and audit-level logs in the console. we can share the security pack after the call.

[00:11:30] [00:11:30] Sofia: last demo — simulate a client timeout during a fallback. starting a session that will exceed the load balancer idle timeout and see the reconnect behavior.
[00:11:42] [00:11:42] Sofia: at 00:11:55 the LB closed the socket, client tried to reconnect, session rehydration took ~750ms and some earlier tokens were re-requested. the rerun shows duplicate ids which the runtime de-duplicates if clients include idempotency keys.
[00:12:10] Evan: so best practice is idempotent chunks and client checkpointing?
[00:12:14] Jordan: exactly. also capture chunk metadata and if you need strict exactly-once semantics we can help design a small gateway layer.

[00:12:26] Priya: ok this was super helpful. what's next? we'd like Redwood to run that 1-hour spike on our sample traces and then a run with a 250k token trace.
[00:12:36] Jordan: noted. Sofia will run the stress tests and we'll share a result dashboard. Jordan will follow up with pricing and an SLA addendum. Marcus will coordinate VPC peering.

[00:12:48] [00:12:48] Jordan: any final questions?
[00:12:50] Evan: just one — do you have a recommended config for KeepAlive and LB settings to align with your defaults?
[00:12:56] Sofia: yes we'll share a small runbook: LB idle 90s, keepalive 25s, fd limit 65k, and per-conn inflight default 32. that's in the follow-up.

[00:13:10] Jordan: thanks everyone we'll send the follow-ups.

Recap / Next steps:
- Sofia to run 1-hour 5k TPS spike with Monarch sample traces and share raw logs and dashboard (due 2026-12-22).
- Jordan to send pricing tiers, SLA addendum and security pack (due 2026-12-20).
